title: REST API Design
subtitle: Resource-oriented noun hierarchies, HTTP method semantics, RFC 7807 error envelopes, and modeling non-CRUD actions.
keyTakeaways: RESTful APIs structure URIs around plural nouns (`/v1/orders`), mapping actions to standard HTTP verbs rather than embedding verbs in endpoints (`/createOrder`).
Non-CRUD actions (such as order cancellation or checkout) are cleanly modeled as state machine transitions or dedicated sub-resources (`POST /orders/{id}/cancellation`).
Long-running operations should return `202 Accepted` immediately with a `Location: /jobs/{id}` status URL and `Retry-After` header to avoid holding open client connections.
architectureDiagram:
RESTFUL RESOURCE HIERARCHY & ASYNC POLLING PATTERN
CRUD Operations on Collections:
  GET    /api/v1/orders              -> List orders (200 OK)
  POST   /api/v1/orders              -> Create order (201 Created + Location header)
  GET    /api/v1/orders/{orderId}    -> Fetch single order (200 OK / 404 Not Found)
  DELETE /api/v1/orders/{orderId}    -> Cancel/Delete order (204 No Content)

Long-Running Asynchronous Processing:
  POST /api/v1/video-exports         -> 202 Accepted (Location: /api/v1/jobs/j_99)
  GET  /api/v1/jobs/j_99             -> 200 OK (Status: "PROCESSING", Progress: 45%)
  GET  /api/v1/jobs/j_99             -> 303 See Other (Location: /api/v1/downloads/v_99)

sections.heading: Resource Modeling, Nesting Depth, and Non-CRUD Actions
sections.body: A clean REST API models business entities as resources identified by nouns, using HTTP verbs to convey intent. A common mistake is deep URL nesting like `/orgs/{id}/departments/{id}/teams/{id}/members/{id}`, which tightly couples endpoint URLs to internal database foreign key schemas and creates brittle client integrations. In production, nest resources at most one level deep (`/teams/{teamId}/members`); everything else should be queryable by top-level identifiers (`/members/{memberId}`).
bullets: Plural Nouns: Use `/v1/users` and `/v1/accounts`, avoiding RPC-style verbs like `/getUser` or `/deleteAccount`.
Nesting Depth Limit: Keep hierarchy shallow. Use `/orders/{orderId}/items`, but fetch individual line items directly at `/items/{itemId}`.

Non-CRUD State Transitions: When an action doesn't fit standard PUT/PATCH (e.g., executing a checkout or approving a transfer), treat the action as a sub-resource: `POST /orders/{id}/payments` or `POST /transfers/{id}/approval`.

sections.heading: Handling Long-Running Asynchronous Operations
sections.body: HTTP is designed for fast request-response exchanges. When an endpoint triggers a heavy operation like generating a monthly PDF invoice or training a machine learning model, holding the client's HTTP connection open for 45 seconds causes proxy timeouts (504s), connection resets, and client retries that crush backend workers. REST handles this via the `202 Accepted` pattern.
bullets: Admission & 202 Accepted: Validate inputs, enqueue the background job, and immediately return HTTP 202 with a `Location: /jobs/{jobId}` header.
Status Polling: The client polls `/jobs/{jobId}`. While running, the server returns 200 with metadata (`{"status": "in_progress", "progress": 65}`) and a `Retry-After: 5` header.
Completion & Redirection: When finished, the status endpoint returns an HTTP 303 See Other pointing directly to the generated resource (`Location: /invoices/inv_102.pdf`).

tradeOffs.pros: Simpler client integration; client receives final output in one round trip; zero background queue infrastructure required.
tradeOffs.cons: Vulnerable to client and proxy timeouts on slow operations; exhausts server worker threads during traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Simple CRUD operations completing in under 200ms (reading profile, updating address, inserting record).

tradeOffs.pros: Protects API servers from timeouts; decouples work submission from worker fleet execution; absorbs massive traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires clients to manage polling loops or WebSockets; requires persistent job storage to track state.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Video processing, large CSV data exports, report generation, and third-party webhook verification.

interviewTip: When designing an API that processes long-running workflows, describe the exact HTTP handoff: 'The API will return a 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to the job status endpoint and a Retry-After header. Once processing completes, the job endpoint returns a 303 See Other redirecting to the completed resource.'
